To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the extinction of a conditioned response is stimulus specific and is dependent on the time of the stimulus.

a conditioned response (e.g., a conditioned nictitating-membrane response) can be selectively extinguished in a particular portion of the conditioned stimulus (e.g., the first 200 ms of a 500-ms tone) while the response is still paired with an unconditioned stimulus.

the conditioned response (CR), which was originally acquired with two stimuli and two interstimulus intervals, could be selectively extinguished in one stimulus (CSA) but not in the other stimulus (CSB) in which the shorter interstimulus interval was maintained.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of learning.
the question of how the brain stores information about time.

the question of whether the extinction of a conditioned response can be selective, in the sense of being limited to a particular component of the stimulus complex that is paired with the unconditoned stimulus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the extinction effect in this preparation is not due to a simple habituation effect, and is not a result of a generalization decrement, but rather is a result of a time-based learning process.
, at least in the rabbit nCMR preparation, a CS can be divided into two or more portions and each portion can be trained to be a separate CS.
extinction of a CR does not occur when the CR is paired with the US.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CR is a function of the time of occurrence of the US.
extinction can occur in the absence of the US if the CS is presented in the same temporal relationship with the US.
, in the conditioned nictitation preparation, extinction can be stimulus specific, but only in the early portion of a CS.
The main takeaway from our work is that

extinction of a conditioned response (e.g., a fear response to a conditioned stimulus, CS) can occur without the extinction of the unconditioned response (e.g. fear to the unconditioned stimulis, US).
the extinction of the CR is not a simple process.
extinction of the CR can occur for a particular portion of the CS, leaving the remainder intact, and that this can be achieved with a single CS-US pairing.
